source.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
source.authors: Danny Hernandez; Tom B. Brown; Tom Conerly; Nova DasSarma; Dawn Drain; Sheer El Showk; Nelson Elhage; Zac Hatfield-Dodds; T. Henighan; Tristan Hume; Scott Johnston; B. Mann; Chris Olah; Catherine Olsson; D. Amodei; Nicholas Joseph; J. Kaplan; Sam McCandlish

page_placements.theme: Training data effects on copying ability

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices and references, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies repeated-data training and measures prefix matching, copying, and token-index loss to test how induction-head-associated behavior changes; it does not reproduce induction-head formation or the original training-time phase-change analysis.
record.gate_note: The study measures prefix matching as an induction-head-related score, copying, and in-context-learning loss. Its scaling-law results and claims cited from other work are not rows. The one-layer skip-trigram copying result is recorded under fits_no_version because it is not an induction-head result.
record.test_reason: The study trains models on mostly unique data plus a repeated subset and measures induction-head prefix-matching score, copying loss and token-index loss. These are results on whether induction heads and in-context learning persist depending on training data (V5). It does not test the composition mechanism, formation timing, or induction heads' share of in-context learning in large models.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that repeated data disproportionately damages copying and induction heads (prefix-matching score), with in-context learning also harmed, and that this co-occurrence adds evidence for induction heads as the source of in-context learning. They suggest that in a 2-layer model a skip-trigram head replaced the induction head. They concede that the logit attribution was inconclusive and that prefix-matching results are less conclusive than the copying results.
record.recipe_differences: The prefix-matching score follows the measurement described by Olsson et al.; this study varies repeated-data training and measures damage rather than studying induction-head formation during ordinary training.
record.method_sensitivity: Prefix-matching and copying damage varies with repeated-data fraction and repetition frequency; the authors report preferential prefix-matching damage at low repeated-data fractions rather than across the entire range.

fits_no_version.finding: In a 1-layer attention-only model, repeated-data training sharply reduced skip-trigram copying of recurring names (above 97% vs below 4%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Repeated-data training impairs one-layer skip-trigram copying.

record.problems: The mechanistic inspection is limited to one- and two-layer attention-only models, with some copying examples qualitative and selected. The authors report noisy fits for some scans and could not clearly resolve the source of the two-layer attribution differences. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the claim-relevant results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant numerical results omitted. Scaling-law, Python-loss, and fine-tuning results do not directly measure induction-head behavior or the claimed token-index mechanism.

untested.parts: No test of composition with a previous-token head or of the [A][B]…[A]→[B] circuit. Prefix matching and copying are only used as induction-head proxies.
No training-time measurement of when induction heads form or of a co-occurring in-context-learning gain or loss bump.
In-context learning by token index is measured only in a 2-layer model. The authors' claim that co-occurrence bolsters V3 rests on correlation only, with no causal test in large models.
No cross-family or cross-modality prevalence test.
Only repeated-data fraction and repetition frequency are varied. Formation timing, other data properties and regularisation are not studied.

missing.what: Loss on the Xth consecutive copy of the paragraph does not decrease at all at the double-descent peak (2-layer, 50% repeated). This is confirmed with a 125-character paragraph.
The authors claim that in the 2-layer model a skip-trigram head appears to have replaced the induction head entirely. This is stated without a quantitative result.
Prefix-matching score vs model size for control models and under 90% repetition, and the model-size-averaged prefix-matching multiplier vs repeated fraction.

record.verdict_notes: V1 links were removed from all rows: the study assumes the induction-head mechanism and uses prefix matching as a proxy, without testing composition. The paper's prefix-matching magnitudes are internally inconsistent (2x in the text, 1.47 in the Fig. 6 caption, 32% in the summary). No uncertainty estimates are reported, and the 2-layer per-token examples are selected. Tranche T3: a new setting (data repetition) with results on V5. V3 is discussed by the authors but not tested in large models.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish formation by composition with a previous-token head; it measures prefix matching and copying, including in a two-layer attention-only model.
No measurement of induction-head formation over training time or whether it coincides with an in-context-learning gain or training-loss bump.
Does not establish that induction heads carry most in-context learning in large transformers; no causal comparison of induction heads with other mechanisms or few-shot task learning.
Does not test prevalence across model families, independent training runs, other architectures, or modalities.
Tests repeated-data fraction and repetition frequency, not other data properties or training setups; does not map when heads first form during training.
Does not compare few-shot task learning with other heads or mechanisms.
Does not resolve whether induction-head formation consists of multiple sub-steps or overlapping transitions.

rows.subject: models trained on repeated data; aggregate across model sizes
rows.size_stated: varied; 1,570,000 to 805,000,000 parameters in the prefix-matching scan
rows.operation_detail: Train with varying repeated-data fractions and repetition frequencies; evaluate prefix-matching score at the double-descent peak and compare with unique-data control scan.
rows.measure: Effective model-size decrease implied by prefix-matching score
rows.baseline: Control-model prefix-matching score fit; general test-loss decrease stated for comparison as 1.15x
rows.value: 2x effective parameter decrease in prefix matching score
rows.note: The authors say the prefix-matching damage is preferential at low repeated-data fractions and is not present across the entire range.
rows.check: Not a V1 test, since it does not measure composition or the copying mechanism; it bears on V5. The paper's numbers disagree: the text says 2x, Fig. 6 caption says a 1.47 multiplier, and the summary says a 32% average reduction. Preferential damage appears only at low repeated fractions (about 3–20%).

source_check.correct: At 3% repeated tokens, the Results prose reports a 2x effective-parameter decrease without identifying it as an average. Figure 6 reports an average 1.47-fold reduction; the summary reports an average 32% reduction. The latter two are approximately equivalent.
source_check.locator_found: Summary of Results, lines 175–179; Figure 6 caption, lines 712–720; Results, lines 730–735.
source_check.problem: The row attributes averaging across model sizes to the prose's 2x result; the explicitly averaged estimates are different.

rows.subject: 1.5M parameter model
rows.stage_stated: trained on repeated data; evaluated at the double-descent peak
rows.operation_detail: Train with repeated data and measure prefix matching and paragraph copying.
rows.measure: Effective model size implied by prefix-matching score
rows.value: Equivalent prefix-matching score to a model with effectively 2,000 parameters
rows.note: The text also says paragraph-level copying completely broke down in this condition; that copying result is not separately quantified here.
rows.check: Drop V1. Prefix matching fell to the level of a 2,000-parameter model, against 30,000 parameters on overall loss, at 50% repetition, with paragraph copying completely broken down. This is a single selected model.

relation.reason: The study intervenes on training-data repetition and measures changes bearing directly on V5.

tranche.reason: Repeated-subset training is a new setting with measured results on V5, including prefix matching and in-context learning.

source_check.notes: The 2x prefix-matching estimate differs from the approximately equivalent averaged estimates of 1.47-fold and 32%. Proper-name probabilities are selected examples; logit attribution did not establish the disruption mechanism.

statements.correction: 3% repetition: Results prose reports 2x; Figure 6 reports an average 1.47-fold reduction; summary reports an average 32% reduction. Preferential prefix-matching damage occurs at low fractions and does not extend across the entire range. A 1.5M model at 50% repetition nevertheless has prefix matching equivalent to 2,000 parameters.
statements.problem: The numerical estimates concern 3% repetition, rather than the stated above-20% condition. A 1.47-fold reduction and a 32% reduction approximately agree. Restricted preferential damage supports V5's dependence claim rather than limiting it; the text does not establish a universal 20% cutoff.

statements.correction: Training repeats a subset of documents. At 3% repeated tokens, the Results prose reports a 2x effective-parameter decrease in prefix matching. At 50%, a 1.5M model matches the prefix score of a 2,000-parameter model. Preferential damage relative to general test loss does not occur across the entire fraction range.
statements.problem: The final sentence changes a restriction on preferential damage into a restriction on damage itself. The paper reports severe prefix-matching degradation at 50% repetition.

statements.correction: The check pack identifies arXiv:2205.10487 as sharing 16 authors with an original. This study provides repeated-data training interventions and results on prefix matching, copying and in-context learning.
statements.problem: The catalog-wide counts cannot be checked from this study. The assertion that the pack does not identify the study sharing authors with an original is contradicted by this pack's explicit header.
